client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last year. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... find reasons not to go, because being there without her feels unbearable. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for taking that brave step to try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that ambivalence makes complete sense. The quiet heaviness in how you're sharing this tells me how much your grandmother meant to you, and how those family gatherings have become painful reminders of her absence rather than sources of comfort. What you're experiencing — that pull to avoid places that highlight her loss — is a very understandable way your mind is trying to protect you from grief, and it's something we can gently explore together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, she was really the center of our family in a lot of ways. When I think about showing up to those gatherings and sitting in her usual chair being empty, or someone else just... casually using her dishes, it makes my chest tighten up and I just can't do it. I guess I hadn't really thought of it as my mind "protecting" me — I just thought I was being weak or selfish for not being there for the rest of my family.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like the words are hard to hold onto — tells me this is sitting very heavily on you right now, and I want to gently push back on that word "weak." What you're describing — the empty chair, her dishes — these aren't small things to brush past; they're profound symbols of someone irreplaceable, and your heart is responding to real loss, not selfishness. In CBT, we'd call that thought — "I'm weak and selfish" — a cognitive distortion worth examining: is there another way to see someone who loves their grandmother so deeply that her absence physically hurts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I mean, when you put it that way, I can kind of see what you're saying — like, maybe it's not weakness, it's just... love that doesn't have anywhere to go anymore. But I'm not sure just reframing it in my head is going to make it easier to actually walk through that door at Thanksgiving. It still feels like the thought and the feeling are two completely different things, and changing one doesn't automatically fix the other.
therapist: What you just said — "love that doesn't have anywhere to go anymore" — is one of the most honest and beautiful descriptions of grief I've heard, and I notice even as you're finding this small insight, there's still a kind of urgency in your voice, like part of you is bracing against the idea that understanding alone won't be enough. You're absolutely right that insight and feeling are different things — CBT doesn't ask you to think your way out of grief, but rather to slowly, gently build small experiences that show your nervous system it can survive walking through that door. We might think about what one tiny, manageable step toward Thanksgiving could look like — not erasing the pain, but learning that you can carry it and still show up.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about small steps, but I honestly don't know what that even looks like — like, do I just show up for an hour and then leave? Because part of me worries that if I go and then fall apart in front of everyone, it'll make them feel worse too, and then I'll just feel guilty on top of everything else. The grief is already so heavy, and the idea of adding guilt about ruining someone else's holiday on top of it feels like too much to risk.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a kind of urgency — tells me this fear is very alive in you in this moment, not just an abstract worry. I want to gently name something: you're carrying grief *and* pre-emptively taking responsibility for everyone else's emotional experience, which is an enormous weight to place on yourself — and it's worth asking whether your family might actually find comfort in grieving *together* with you, rather than needing you to hold it together for them. Yes, showing up for just an hour is absolutely a valid small step — and "falling apart" in front of people who loved her too might look less like ruining a holiday and more like giving everyone permission to miss her honestly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That idea — giving everyone permission to miss her — I hadn't thought of it that way, and it actually made me tear up a little, so maybe there's something to it. But I also know my family, and we're not really the type to cry together openly — my mom especially tends to just push through and act like everything's fine, so I worry I'd be the only one falling apart and it would just feel embarrassing. I guess I'm not totally convinced that my family would respond the way you're describing, even if the idea sounds nice in theory.
therapist: The fact that this idea moved you to tears — even briefly — tells me it touched something real and true in you, even if your mind is quickly stepping in with very valid concerns about your family's actual dynamics. That tension you're feeling, between what *could* be healing and what you realistically know about your mom and your family's patterns, is worth honoring rather than dismissing — you know your family, and I'm not here to paint an idealized picture. But I'm curious: even if others don't cry with you, is there a difference between being *embarrassed* by your grief and being *wrong* to have it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because no — I don't think I'm wrong to grieve her, I know she deserved to be grieved. But embarrassment feels so real in the moment that it kind of doesn't matter if it's "logical" or not — like, my face going red and everyone looking at me would still feel awful even if I intellectually knew I had every right to cry. I guess I'm realizing the fear isn't really about being wrong, it's more about being seen in a vulnerable way by people who might not meet me there.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — your voice high and quick, like you're working something out in real time — matches this moment perfectly, because what you just named is genuinely important: the fear isn't about being *wrong*, it's about being *exposed* in a space that may not feel safe enough to hold you. That is such a precise and self-aware insight, and it shifts the question from "do I have the right to grieve" to something more tender — "how do I let myself be seen when I'm not sure I'll be caught." That's not a logic problem to solve; that's about trust, and it's worth exploring what it would take — even in small ways — to feel just a little safer being vulnerable at that gathering.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think what would help is having at least one person there who I know gets it — like my cousin Dara, she was really close to my grandmother too, and I've actually been avoiding her calls lately, which I feel terrible about. Maybe if I talked to her before Thanksgiving, I'd feel less alone walking in, but honestly I've been putting it off because even that conversation feels like opening a door I'm not sure I'm ready to go through. It's like every path toward feeling better requires me to be vulnerable first, and that part keeps tripping me up.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now feels like someone standing at the edge of something — and what you've just mapped out is actually a really meaningful path forward, because reaching out to Dara isn't a grand gesture, it's one honest conversation with someone who is probably also sitting by her phone missing her cousin and missing your grandmother. You've named the pattern so clearly: vulnerability feels like the price of every step toward healing, and that cost feels high — but I wonder if Dara picking up that call might feel less like opening a scary door and more like two people finally exhaling together. What would it feel like to text her today, just to say "I've been thinking about you"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, just imagining sending that text made my stomach drop a little, which I know probably sounds ridiculous for something so small. Part of me worries that once I open that door with Dara, she'll want to talk about everything all at once, and I'm not sure I can handle that — like what if she's been holding a lot too and it becomes this overwhelming flood? I guess I could try to just keep it short and not commit to a big conversation right away, but I'm not totally sure I trust myself to hold that boundary once emotions get involved.
therapist: The tightness in your voice right now — high and fast, like you're already bracing for that flood — tells me this fear is very real, not ridiculous at all, and it makes complete sense that even imagining the text brought that stomach drop. But I want to reflect something back to you: you just spontaneously came up with a wise, boundaried approach — keep it short, don't commit to a big conversation — which means part of you already knows how to protect yourself here, even if you don't fully trust it yet. What if the goal of that text isn't to open every door at once, but just to let Dara know she's not alone — and to remind yourself that you get to control the pace of this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think you're right that I came up with that on my own, and maybe I'm selling myself short when it comes to knowing my own limits. But "you get to control the pace" is one of those things that sounds true in theory and then completely falls apart for me in practice — like, I've told myself I'd keep things brief before and then ended up in a two-hour phone call feeling wrung out. I guess I'm just not sure I trust myself to follow through on the boundary when I'm actually in the middle of feeling something.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're speaking quickly, tells me this isn't frustration — it's something quieter, like a kind of tired honesty about a pattern you've lived enough times to stop trusting yourself around. And that history is real and worth respecting — but I'd gently offer that "keeping it brief" in the past may have felt like a rule you were trying to enforce alone, whereas this time you'd be going in with something different: a specific, conscious reason to pace yourself, which is protecting your ability to actually show up at Thanksgiving. What if instead of relying on willpower in the moment, you gave yourself a concrete out beforehand — something like telling Dara upfront, "I've missed you and I want to talk, but I only have about 20 minutes today"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's actually a really practical idea, and I like that it gives me something concrete to say instead of just hoping I'll find the willpower in the moment. I guess my worry is that Dara might take it the wrong way — like, she might feel like I'm putting a timer on our grief, or that I'm not fully showing up for her. But maybe that's me catastrophizing again, and she'd probably just be relieved to hear from me at all.
therapist: The way you're speaking — measured, thoughtful, almost like you're carefully weighing each word — tells me something has shifted slightly; you're not bracing or rushing anymore, you're actually thinking this through. And notice what just happened: you caught your own catastrophizing, named it, and then offered yourself a more balanced perspective entirely on your own — that's a real CBT skill working in real time, not something I did. Dara has likely been missing you and your shared grief, and "I only have 20 minutes today" is far more likely to sound like care than rejection to someone who loves you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
